answer: According to the DeepWalk paper (Perozzi, Al-Rfou, and Skiena, 2014), the learned representations are latent, low-dimensional vector embeddings of the nodes, learned by treating truncated random walks over the graph as sentences and applying a skip-gram language model. Their key properties are: they are scalable (online and incremental, so they can be updated as the graph changes without retraining from scratch), they are dense and low-dimensional, and they are robust to sparsity and missing information. Regarding community structure, the paper reports that the representations encode community membership: nodes in the same community or densely connected region end up close together in the latent space, so the embeddings capture community structure and support community classification, even when the community information is not directly given. Regarding network changes, because the method is incremental (new nodes can be added and new walks trained with the existing model via online learning), the representations can be updated efficiently as the network evolves, and the paper notes this makes the approach suitable for dynamic or evolving networks.
confidence_reasoning: The general claims (latent low-dimensional embeddings, community membership encoded, online/incremental updates, scalability and robustness) match my recollection of the DeepWalk paper, but I am not certain of exact wording or which specific properties the paper emphasizes.
